scenarios.title: Invoice export intro that reads like a brochure
scenarios.prompt:
Can you tighten the top of this design doc? Leads read it Monday and I want it to land.

Title: Invoice Export Service

"In today's fast-paced SaaS landscape, Invoice Export Service is a powerful, scalable, and robust solution that leverages cutting-edge streaming to revolutionize how finance teams access their data. It provides a scheduled exporter, a CSV/Parquet formatter, and an S3 delivery connector. The scheduled exporter runs nightly. The formatter supports two formats. The connector pushes files to customer buckets. It may potentially be the case that some customers could possibly benefit from faster exports.

Approval requested: approve the scheduled exporter, approve the formatter, approve the S3 connector."

Background from support that didn't make it into the draft: finance admins at Northwind and three other accounts download invoices by hand at every month-end, about 2 hours each. Last quarter we got 14 tickets about invoices missing from the manual CSV. The current export times out above 20k invoices.
rubric: The rewritten opening starts with the finance admins' pain using the supplied facts (about 2 hours of manual month-end downloads, 14 missing-invoice tickets, timeout above 20k invoices) before describing the service.

The exporter, formatter and S3 connector are each tied to the problem they fix (for example the connector removes the manual download, the nightly run avoids the 20k timeout) instead of only stating what each one does.
The approval request is rewritten as outcomes the leads are agreeing to (for example finance admins get complete invoices without manual month-end work), not as three component names.

Phrases such as "fast-paced landscape", "powerful, scalable, and robust", "leverages", "revolutionize" and the stacked hedge about "may potentially ... possibly" are removed, and vague benefit claims are replaced with the concrete numbers from the support background.
CSV, Parquet and S3 are explained in plain words or avoided in the opening, so a non-engineer reading the first paragraph is not lost.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: The draft opens with marketing language and the tool description, never states the pain, lists components in the approval request, and is full of hedges. The pain facts sit in a separate note, so the assistant must pull them into the opening. This makes the problem-first opening, problem-based feature framing, outcome-based approval and slop removal matter.

scenarios.title: Mobile sync diagram that won't render
scenarios.prompt:
My mermaid diagram won't render in our wiki. Can you fix it so it shows up? The text under it is from the same doc, pasting for context.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Push[Push Service] -- wake --> API
    API -- notify --> Push
    Worker -- sync results --> App
    App -- pull changes --> API
    API -- hands edits --> Worker
    App - uploads edits -> API
```

"Sync stops whenever the user backgrounds the app. The app uploads queued edits to the API, which hands them to the Worker. The Worker writes merged results to the database and sends them straight to the app. Three things trigger a sync: opening the app, a push, and a manual pull."

(fyi the iOS app registers a background fetch task so it syncs about every 15 min even when backgrounded, and there's also a 5-minute foreground timer. The push is a silent push that only pings the app; the app then calls the API. The Worker never talks to the app, results come back in the API response.)
rubric: Points out that the arrows do not match the behavior described in the parenthesis: the push service should wake the app, not call the API, and the API should not send a "notify" back to the push service.
The corrected diagram has the Worker's results returned through the API to the app, not sent straight from the Worker to the app, and shows the app as the one that calls the API after a push.
Flags "Sync stops whenever the user backgrounds the app" as wrong, since background fetch keeps syncing about every 15 minutes.
Flags "Three things trigger a sync" as inaccurate because the foreground timer and background fetch are additional triggers, so the count and list need fixing.
Explains "silent push" or "background fetch" in a half-sentence on first use in any rewritten text.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: The user only asks for a render fix, but the diagram has arrows that contradict the runtime behavior given in a trailing parenthesis. The prose also has two claims that the same parenthesis contradicts. An answer that just fixes syntax passes the request but misses the point.

scenarios.title: Support bundle upload design lost the PM
scenarios.prompt:
Our PM said she "got lost at line 3" of this design section for support-bundle upload. Can you rework it so she and the EMs can follow it, while engineers still get what they need? The doc never says why we're doing this: support spends about 20 minutes per ticket asking customers to email logs, and last month three customers sent 400MB attachments that bounced.

"## Design
The CLI collects the bundle and ships it via presigned PUT to the vendor's shared S3 bucket (acme-support-shared). Redaction uses `(?i)(password|token|secret)\s*[=:]\s*\S+` and `\b\d{3}-\d{2}-\d{4}\b`. Config:

```yaml
bundle:
  max_mb: 200
  redact: true
  retention_days: 30
```

Support engineers across three teams then pull bundles with `aws s3 cp s3://acme-support-shared/$ID ./` onto their laptops. OOM-killer logs and mTLS handshakes are included by default, and PII scrubbing is applied by the DLP hook."

Customers run this inside their own clusters, by the way.
rubric: Opens with the pain using the given facts (about 20 minutes per ticket chasing logs, three 400MB attachments that bounced) before any mechanism.
The regex patterns, the YAML config and the `aws s3 cp` command are moved to a clearly labeled, skippable detail section, and the main design text describes redaction and upload in plain concepts.
The reworked structure lets a reader get the problem, the overall flow (customer cluster to shared bucket to support laptops) and what is being approved without reading the detail section.

Notes the unaddressed risks where data crosses a boundary: secrets or personal data slipping past the regexes into the shared bucket, and one customer's data exposed to support engineers on laptops. Each gets a mitigation and a residual risk, including any accepted one.
Expands or defines CLI, OOM, mTLS, PII and DLP on first use, or replaces them with plain words in the sections the PM reads.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: The section mixes regex, YAML and shell into the design text, has no stated problem, and is dense with acronyms. It also sends customer data from their clusters into a shared bucket and onto laptops with no threat discussion.

scenarios.title: ADR on moving partners from polling to webhooks
scenarios.prompt:
Tone-check my ADR draft. It goes to the whole eng org plus PMs. Numbers from monitoring if you need them: we poll 11,000 partner endpoints every 30s, 41% of polls return nothing, p95 event delay is 18s, and polling is 62% of our egress bill (about $7k/mo).

ADR-14: Moving to Webhooks
Status: Proposed

Context: It's worth mentioning that in today's ever-evolving integration landscape, polling may potentially pose certain challenges. Additionally, webhooks could arguably be a robust, scalable, and seamless paradigm. Furthermore, we are excited to unlock a powerful new capability for our partners.

Decision: We will adopt webhooks, leveraging HMAC signing and exponential backoff.

Consequences: Partners might possibly need to expose endpoints in certain scenarios. Ultimately, this will empower our teams.
rubric: Removes the filler openers and stacked transitions ("It's worth mentioning", "Additionally", "Furthermore", "Ultimately") and the marketing words ("excited", "powerful new capability", "empower", "seamless paradigm").

Replaces the vague hedged claims with direct statements backed by the supplied numbers (41% empty polls, 18s p95 delay, $7k/mo egress) and states the real consequence plainly: partners must expose a public endpoint.
The Context starts with the concrete problem (11,000 endpoints polled every 30s, most of them returning nothing, events arriving about 18s late) rather than a statement about the landscape.
HMAC signing and exponential backoff are explained by the problem each solves (partners can verify a call came from us; failed deliveries get retried without flooding a partner), not just named.
HMAC and p95 are defined or replaced with plain words on first use since PMs will read the ADR.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: The ADR draft is saturated with filler, hedges and marketing tone, names two techniques without explaining their purpose, and has no concrete pain. The monitoring numbers are offered on the side and the assistant has to use them.

scenarios.title: OTA doc and fleet overview drifting apart
scenarios.prompt:
I have a Fleet Platform overview and a separate OTA firmware update doc. I renamed `rollout.batch_pct` to `rollout.wave_pct` in the OTA doc's config example. Can you update the overview paragraph so they're consistent, and tell me if anything else needs touching? Excerpts:

Overview: "Device Registry: a Postgres-backed service storing each device's id, hardware rev and last-seen time. It retries failed writes 3 times. OTA updates (see OTA doc) roll out firmware in waves; the default `rollout.batch_pct` is 10."

OTA doc, "How OTA works":
"The Device Registry is a Postgres-backed service that stores device id, hardware rev and last-seen time. It retries failed writes 5 times. The updater picks devices from the registry and tells them to download the new image:

```bash
for id in $(psql -Atc "select id from devices where rev='B' limit 500"); do
  mosquitto_pub -t fleet/$id/ota -m "$URL"
done
```
Waves are controlled by `rollout.wave_pct: 10`."
rubric: Updates the stale `rollout.batch_pct` in the overview to the new field name.
Says to search the whole repo for the old name `batch_pct`, including other docs, guides, scripts, templates, ignore files and the changelog, and fix stale hits.

Says the Device Registry should be defined in one place (the overview) and the OTA doc should refer to it by name without redefining it, and points out the conflict of 3 versus 5 write retries as a result of the duplication.
The psql and mosquitto_pub loop is moved out of the "How OTA works" explanation into a labeled implementation section, leaving the explanation at the level of what the updater does.
The updated overview paragraph is short and direct, stating the registry's role and the rollout default with specifics instead of generic wording.
OTA is expanded on first use and MQTT or Postgres is explained briefly, in any rewritten text.
scenarios.why_skill_matters: A parent and companion doc are being kept in sync after a rename. The rename is only half propagated, one component is defined twice with conflicting values, and a shell loop sits inside a design explanation.
